title: Is your Linux display really showing 10-bit color?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You bought an HDR 4K monitor, plugged it into a Linux machine, and the settings say it's fine. But is it really showing ten bits per channel?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'd have assumed so. How would you even check?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's what Antoine's small project, HDR-10bpp-Display-Test, is for. It checks HDR 4K display on Linux, including ten bits per channel, so you can validate the graphics stack, the drivers and the monitor.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You need an X server, Python 3, GTK 3, ImageJ for showing ten-bit images, and ImageIO for reading them. Then you stop the display manager and the X server, and restart X with a color depth of thirty.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Thirty bits, so ten per channel.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. You confirm the depth with a quick check on the root window, launch the viewer, which has a version for video, and open an image in ImageJ. If the colors look accurate, the chain works.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And if X won't start at thirty?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The page suggests trying a depth of twenty-four instead. That's a useful clue in itself, since it means something in the stack can't do ten bits.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: MIT. The full project page has the exact steps and the repository link.
